paragraphs.text: Before you begin
Moses Afolabi • Illustrated edition • 2026

Read the whole Bible passage before working through a chapter. Scripture quotations use the King James Version. Modern application scenes and illustrations are teaching examples. They do not describe documented events or verified personal testimonies.
Historical accounts are identified and accompanied by source links. Consider their particular setting as you reflect on the biblical passage.

Take time to read the explanation, study the visual summary, and complete the practice in your own notebook. Discuss difficult questions with a trusted pastor or mature believer. Return to the chapter after trying its suggested action.
The PDF contains still illustrations. The separate animated companion adds gentle motion and chapter prompts.

Chapter 1 Tell the truth about the hurt
Bring an honest account to God. Name what is known, its effect, and the help you need without inventing another person’s motives.
Read Scripture in its setting
How long wilt thou forget me, O LORD? for ever? how long wilt thou hide thy face from me? — Psalm 13:1, KJV

Psalm 13 gives a sufferer language for speaking to God. Its questions are followed by requests and then an expression of trust. Read all six verses and allow each movement its proper place. Trust does not require a false description of the wound. Begin with the event and the need you can actually name, then ask for help with the response before you. A person may remain with one sentence of lament before finding words for the next.
The practical situation

The recurring fictional case concerns Martha, whose cousin Lydia shared information Martha had asked her to keep private. The story illustrates an ordinary breach of confidence. It is not a model for managing abuse or danger. The practical exercises remain optional, and private writing or direct contact can be omitted where unsafe.
Biblical testimony · Hannah speaks from her distress

Read 1 Samuel 1:9–18. Hannah comes before the Lord with grief and speaks from her heart. Eli initially misunderstands what he sees; Hannah explains her distress. The account lets us notice the difference between a person’s outward appearance and what they are carrying. We should hear an account before assigning a motive to someone’s tears.

Hannah’s particular circumstances and later answer belong to her story. They do not establish a timetable for another person’s relief. The practical invitation is to bring an honest request to God and seek a trustworthy listener who will take the concern seriously. Ask what you need the listener to understand before they offer an interpretation.
Let yourself name what the event cost

The impact of a hurt can extend beyond the first moment. Consider what changed in your willingness to speak, how you entered a gathering, or what responsibilities became harder to carry. Put a name to one effect you can describe. A specific effect often gives you a more useful starting point for prayer.

Martha noticed that she had stopped responding to ordinary messages in the family chat. She still wanted to know about birthdays and gatherings. She wanted her financial details to stay private. These two facts helped her see that she could mute one conversation for a time while remaining connected to a relative she trusted.

Exercise. Complete the sentence “Since it happened, I have found it harder to ____.” Choose one effect to bring before God. Then write one thing you would like to protect in the coming week. Keep the two sentences somewhere appropriate to your circumstances.
Pray the movements of Psalm 13

The psalm begins with questions, turns toward a request, and closes with trust. Try praying in that order. Let your first sentence say what is hard, let the second name the help you need, and let the last remember something true about God. You can spend time with one movement and return to another later.

Martha asked how long she would feel uneasy at family gatherings. She asked the Lord for courage to talk with someone who would listen. She closed by remembering His steadfast love. A few days later she prayed the same Psalm and had a clearer request about an upcoming dinner.

Exercise. Read all six verses. Write a question, a request, and a sentence of trust. Read the lines slowly as a prayer. If you have only a question today, bring it to God and use the Psalm to return when you have words for the next part.
Choose the right audience for the story

You may need someone to listen, someone with responsibility to act, or someone with particular training. Ask what you want from the conversation before choosing whom to approach. A friend can listen and pray. A person responsible for a report or concern may need a clear account and relevant details.

Martha asked a trusted relative to hear what had happened. She explained that she wanted help thinking through a response and asked the relative to keep the conversation private. Later, she addressed the ongoing discussion directly with the person who could stop spreading the information. The two conversations had different purposes.

Exercise. Name one kind of help you need and one person suited to offer it. Decide what details they need to hear. Prepare one sentence asking for the kind of help you want. Give them room to say what they are able to provide.
Visual summary
State the event accurately
Name its effect honestly
Bring the need before God
Apply one step to a situation you face today.
Review the account before you act

Return to the account after you have had time to pray or think. Check which parts remain clear and which depend on an assumption. Ask whether the step you are considering addresses what happened. If the facts are unclear or contact is unwise, a private prayer or conversation with a trustworthy person may be enough for now.

Martha reread her three sentences before deciding whether to speak with Lydia. She removed a line about Lydia's motive that she could not verify. She kept the sentence about the promise of privacy and the effect of hearing the detail at dinner. That was enough to describe why she wanted the disclosure to stop.
Use the Truth and Impact worksheet. Record the event, what it cost, what remains unclear, and what you need now. Pray for courage to tell the truth and wisdom about whom to tell.
Prayer. Father, You see what happened and what it cost me. Give me courage to bring You the truth and grace to hear what I need for the next step. Amen.
Chapter 2 Remember the mercy you received
Remember Christ’s mercy while choosing your own response. Truth and kindness can be practiced together.
Read Scripture in its setting
And be ye kind one to another, tenderhearted, forgiving one another, even as God for Christ's sake hath forgiven you. — Ephesians 4:32, KJV

Paul locates the ground of forgiveness in God’s mercy in Christ. Read the instruction within the whole paragraph on truth, anger, useful work, and speech that builds up. Grace reaches a real life with particular actions. Remembering mercy can influence the manner of your response while leaving the facts of the injury intact. You can speak clearly about a wrong and refuse to use that truth as an excuse to cause another wrong.
The practical situation

Martha wants to remember Christ’s mercy without minimizing the disclosure of her private information. Her task is to choose a truthful response she can own. Lydia remains responsible for her own conduct and any repair that belongs to her.
Biblical parable · The forgiven servant

Read Matthew 18:21–35. Jesus tells a parable about a servant released from an enormous debt who then refuses mercy to a fellow servant. The contrast exposes the failure to let received compassion shape conduct toward another person. Read it as Jesus’ parable and keep the distinction between its imagery and a modern household dispute.

The application calls us to examine our own mercilessness. It does not authorize someone who has harmed us to demand money, secrecy, or renewed access. Ask where the mercy you have received should change a response you control. Then identify any accountability or protection that still needs a responsible place in the plan.
Acknowledge anger and decide what it will do

Anger can draw attention to a real violation. Let it tell you that something matters, then decide how you will respond. Write the action you are tempted to take and ask who would be affected by it. Give yourself a pause if the action could extend the hurt to people who had no part in it.

Martha wanted to answer quickly in the family chat. She chose to wait until she could ask for a specific change. She still felt angry when she returned to the issue. Her message had a smaller audience and a clearer purpose. She could speak with more care because she knew what she wanted to protect.

Exercise. Name the action your anger is urging. Identify one good end you want to reach, such as truth, privacy, or accountability. Choose a response that serves that end and give yourself time to review it before acting.
Make room for truthful mercy

Mercy can shape your tone and the amount of information you share. It can also give you patience to hear a person's account when the conversation is suitable. Keep the action clear. You can acknowledge an explanation and still ask for a particular change in conduct.
Martha heard Lydia say she had mentioned the detail because she thought another relative could help.

Martha could acknowledge the intention and explain that she had given no permission to share it. Lydia had room to take responsibility for the disclosure. Martha could ask her to take one practical step to keep the information from spreading further.

Exercise. Write one sentence describing the harm and one asking for a concrete change. Read them aloud in private. Remove any statement about a motive you cannot know. Keep any useful question that would give the other person room to answer.
Receive mercy for the parts you need to own

A person's hurt can be real while they also recognize something they did poorly in their response. Consider what belongs to you. If you spoke harshly or passed on information you should have kept private, address that action clearly. The other person's conduct still has its own place in the account.

Martha realized she had been short with a relative who had merely asked why she had left the table. She apologized for the way she answered and kept the matter of the disclosure with the people responsible. The apology helped her restore one ordinary connection while the larger issue remained open.

Exercise. Ask whether there is a separate action you need to confess or repair. Name it without taking responsibility for something another person did. If appropriate, offer a brief apology and state what you intend to do differently.
Visual summary
Remember mercy in Christ
Own your particular response
Speak with truth and kindness
Apply one step to a situation you face today.
Return to Christ’s mercy on the next difficult day

A fresh reminder of the hurt can bring anger back. Read the passage again and ask what the mercy you received in Christ invites you to do today. The next action might be a prayer, a careful word, or a return to the boundary you already chose. Give yourself time to keep practicing.

When another message brought the dinner to mind, Martha prayed before answering. She remembered the sentence she had prepared about keeping the matter private. She used it and changed the subject. Afterward she thanked the Lord for the patience to answer plainly.
Use the Mercy and Response worksheet. Name a way you received mercy and one choice it can shape now. Ask the Lord for the courage to speak truthfully and the grace to treat others with care.
Chapter 3 Give up the work of revenge
Pause before sending the message. Ask whether the action protects a real good or mainly promises another injury.
Read Scripture in its setting
Dearly beloved, avenge not yourselves, but rather give place unto wrath: for it is written, Vengeance is mine; I will repay, saith the Lord. — Romans 12:19, KJV

Read verses 17–21 together. Paul directs believers away from personal vengeance and toward good. Entrusting judgment to God changes the purpose of the action you choose. You may still correct a false account, protect someone, or make an appropriate report. Ask whether your planned response serves that purpose or mainly promises another person a taste of your pain. Keep the audience and the information proportionate to the responsibility involved.
The practical situation

Martha notices that a drafted family message contains an unrelated embarrassment about Lydia. The extra detail would create another injury while doing little to stop the original disclosure. She needs a response that addresses the actual harm.
Biblical testimony · David refuses an opportunity for revenge

Read 1 Samuel 24. David has an opportunity to kill Saul and refuses to take it. He later names the circumstances and appeals concerning the wrong done to him. The account distinguishes refusing personal vengeance from pretending that no threat exists. David does not simply resume an unprotected life beside Saul.

This is an ancient account of a particular conflict. It should not be used to require someone today to approach a dangerous person. Its searching question concerns the response within your own control. Can you refuse an unnecessary injury while still taking a responsible step for truth and protection? Seek appropriate support where the situation exceeds what you can safely handle.
Choose one response to practice before you need it

Prepare a short action for the moment anger rises. You might put the phone down, ask for time to answer, or read a sentence you have written about the boundary. Practice the action on a calm day so you can use it when the conversation feels sudden.

Martha chose to mute the chat before drafting any reply to a new message about the dinner. She would come back later and ask whether there was a real question to answer. If she needed another person's help, she would talk privately with the relative she trusted.

Exercise. Finish the line “When I feel the urge to pay someone back, my first step will be ____.” Choose an action you can use without depending on another person. Decide when you will return to the issue and what would make a response worthwhile.
Historical reflection · A call to peace with justice

Abraham Lincoln’s Second Inaugural Address, delivered on March 4, 1865, closes by joining the refusal of malice with charity, firmness about right, care for those harmed by war, and the pursuit of a just peace. The speech addresses a nation nearing the end of civil war. It is a public historical appeal, rather than a complete teaching about personal forgiveness or safety. National Park Service, Lincoln’s Second Inaugural Address

The limited point for reflection is the connection between refusing malice and accepting work that repairs harm. Return to Romans 12 before applying it. Ask which action would serve truth, protection, or responsible care, and which action would mainly cause another injury. Personal mercy need not become indifference to justice.
Let accountability have its proper purpose

Accountability can protect others, correct a false report, or name a responsibility that needs to be carried. Choose the person who can act appropriately and give a factual account. Ask what information they need. Keep the audience proportionate to the purpose.

Martha asked a relative to stop repeating the private detail. Later she asked Lydia to acknowledge the disclosure and help correct it. She did not ask the whole family to decide who was right. The people who could change the conduct heard what she was asking for.

Exercise. Identify one person responsible for addressing the issue and one result you could reasonably request. Describe the event plainly. Ask whether the proposed response belongs with that person, through another appropriate channel, or in a private prayer for now.
Pray about the cost of putting revenge down

Romans 12 calls believers to entrust vengeance to God. Giving up the work of revenge can feel costly when you still want the other person to understand the harm. Bring that desire honestly into prayer. Ask for justice, truth, and the ability to choose what is good in your own conduct.

Martha prayed for the family to understand why privacy mattered. She asked the Lord to keep her from sending a message designed to embarrass someone. Then she took the action she could carry: she asked the appropriate relative to stop discussing her finances. The prayer helped her keep her request clear.

Exercise. Write one sentence about what you wanted retaliation to give you. Turn it into a prayer asking God for the good you need. Follow with one action that reflects truth, care, or a wise boundary.
Visual summary
Recognize the retaliatory impulse
Entrust judgment to God
Choose responsible good
Apply one step to a situation you face today.
Notice what happens after you choose differently

Review the situation after the next difficult moment. Ask whether the alternative action helped you protect the good you intended. If you answered too quickly, identify the point where a pause could help. If the boundary held, record what made it possible and return to that practice.

At the next dinner, Martha used her short sentence and moved the conversation. She still wished the matter had never been shared. She could also see that she had spoken clearly without exposing another person's private story. She wrote down the sentence she wanted to use again.
Use the Revenge and Response worksheet. Record the trigger, the action you chose, and what happened. Thank the Lord for the help you recognized and ask for patience to return to the practice.
Prayer. Lord, You see what is hidden and judge rightly. Help me put down revenge and choose the good I can do today. Amen.
Chapter 4 Give trust time
Seek individualized support where danger or coercion is involved. Forgiveness does not require unsafe contact or renewed access.
Read Scripture in its setting
If it be possible, as much as lieth in you, live peaceably with all men. — Romans 12:18, KJV
A prudent man foreseeth the evil, and hideth himself: but the simple pass on, and are punished. — Proverbs 22:3, KJV
Paul’s wording recognizes the limits of one person’s control. You are responsible for your conduct and cannot guarantee another person’s response. Read

Proverbs 22:3 alongside it. Prudence notices danger and takes shelter. Forgiveness, peace, trust, and access therefore need careful practical distinctions. An apology can be acknowledged while a boundary remains. Decisions about renewed contact should fit observed conduct, safety, and informed support.
The practical situation

In the ordinary fictional family conflict, Lydia acknowledges a disclosure and offers a correction. Martha appreciates that step while keeping sensitive information private. Her situation is distinct from coercion, stalking, threats, or abuse, which require individualized safety support.
Biblical testimony · Judah’s offer becomes visible conduct

Read Genesis 44:18–34 within the longer account of Joseph and his brothers. Judah offers to remain in Benjamin’s place and explains his concern for their father. His words involve a concrete cost he is willing to bear. The passage can help a reader distinguish an expression of regret from conduct that accepts responsibility.

Joseph’s particular methods and authority are part of the ancient narrative, not a template for testing people today. Do not create a dangerous situation to see whether someone has changed. Ask what evidence already exists, what can be observed safely, and whether a proposed change in contact is wise. Keeping the present boundary may remain the appropriate decision.
Choose a boundary you can carry

Name the action you will take, the topic you will keep private, or the contact you are willing to have. A boundary becomes practical when it describes your conduct. Consider what support would help you keep it and whether communicating it is appropriate.

Martha chose to keep financial information private. She prepared a sentence for family conversations and left herself room to step away from the chat if the subject returned. When someone changed the subject after she spoke, she saw that the shorter response was enough for that moment.

Exercise. Complete “When ____ happens, I will ____.” Choose an action you can carry without waiting for agreement. Identify one person who can support you. If sending or speaking the boundary would create risk, seek qualified support before deciding about contact.
Give peace a realistic form

Romans 12 asks believers to pursue peace within the part they can carry. In some situations, peace may look like courteous contact at a gathering. In others it may involve distance and communication through an appropriate person. Ask what arrangement protects safety and truth while leaving room for wise conduct.

Martha kept ordinary contact at family gatherings and chose to keep certain subjects private. She was able to greet Lydia and take part in the meal without treating that contact as proof that every concern had been resolved. The arrangement gave her time to see whether behavior changed.

Exercise. Name a form of contact you can handle and one form you are choosing to leave aside. Decide what would help you keep that arrangement. Give yourself a review date for your own choice without promising anyone renewed access.
Seek specialized support when there is danger

Threats, coercion, stalking, and ongoing abuse call for careful attention to safety. A qualified local advocate can help you think through your circumstances and create a personalized safety plan. If there is immediate danger, seek local emergency help when it is safe to do so. Use a safe way to contact support if you are concerned that someone monitors your communications.

A workbook exercise may be skipped when keeping written notes would be unsafe. Private confrontation and a joint meeting can be left out of a plan where they could increase danger. In situations involving abuse, seek individualized support from a qualified specialist. The ordinary family disagreements in this book use examples suited to those circumstances.

If you are in the United States, the National Domestic Violence Hotline provides safety-planning resources at thehotline.org safety-planning resources . If you are elsewhere, look for a qualified local service from a safe place or device. Choose a safe support step before returning to any exercise about contact.
Visual summary
Attend to safety and truth
Keep an appropriate boundary
Review conduct with wise support
Apply one step to a situation you face today.
Review trust using conduct you have observed

Write down the boundary you have kept and any change in conduct you have actually observed. Give yourself permission to keep the same arrangement if you still need time or support. If you consider a change, describe the smallest change that makes sense for your circumstances.

Martha noticed that Lydia had honored her request in two conversations. She chose to keep sharing ordinary news and to leave financial details private. The decision gave her room to appreciate what had improved while keeping the protection she still wanted.

Use the Boundaries and Trust worksheet only if it is safe to keep a record. Name the arrangement you can carry, the evidence you will watch, and the support you need. Pray for wisdom about what peace can look like in your circumstances.
Prayer. Father, give me wisdom to seek peace faithfully and pay attention to what safety and truth require. Help me receive wise support. Amen.
Chapter 5 Choose a next step
Choose a next step within your control. Appropriate support can help you carry and review it.
Read Scripture in its setting
Put on therefore, as the elect of God, holy and beloved, bowels of mercies, kindness, humbleness of mind, meekness, longsuffering; — Colossians 3:12, KJV

Paul addresses people received by God and describes the character of their shared life. The following verses include forgiveness, love, peace, gratitude, and the word of Christ. A next step can be small and still express that calling. Define an action you can carry rather than an outcome that depends on someone else. Then arrange support and a review suited to the situation. Patience gives room to learn from what actually happens.
The practical situation
Martha prepares a brief sentence to protect her privacy at a gathering and arranges a check-in afterward. She can evaluate whether she kept that boundary even if the gathering still felt difficult.
Biblical testimony · Jesus prays amid wrongdoing

Read Luke 23:32–43. The account records Jesus praying for those involved in His crucifixion, and it also records the reality of the harm done to Him. Christian teaching should leave both visible. His mercy must never be turned into pressure for an injured person to deny suffering or remain exposed to danger.

A reader can begin by praying for help to release personal revenge and to choose what is good. That prayer does not settle every decision about access, reporting, or repair. Name the particular responsibility before you and seek wise support for carrying it. The step can remain faithful even when the other person’s response is outside your control.
Plan what you will do if the moment changes

A conversation may begin earlier than you expected or in a place where you cannot speak freely. Prepare a way to pause or leave the subject. Ask a trustworthy person what help they can offer and confirm when they will be available. Put the options in terms you can remember.

Martha practiced saying, “I'd like to keep that private.” If the conversation continued, she would step away and speak with the relative she had asked for support. She kept the plan small enough to carry while other people were talking around the table.

Exercise. Write your first response and one backup. Decide whom you could contact if you need support afterward. Read both responses privately and use words that sound like something you can actually say.
Let a check-in show what the step taught you

After the planned action, ask what happened and what you learned. Write the result in terms of the action you chose. A conversation can remain difficult even when you speak plainly and protect the boundary you intended to keep. Your review can include both experiences.

Martha noticed that the subject changed after her response. She also felt unsettled when she got home. At the check-in she told her relative both things. The next day she chose to keep the same boundary and pray about what still hurt. The review helped her see an action worth keeping.
Exercise. Write what you expected, what actually happened, and what help you received. Choose whether to repeat the step, adjust it, or seek further support. Put a date beside the decision.
Offer yourself time to return to the work

Colossians 3 connects the work of forgiveness with compassion and patience. Those qualities can guide you as you return to a concern you thought you had already settled. Name what is fresh today. Ask whether it calls for a new action or a return to a practice you have already chosen.

Martha heard the dinner mentioned at a later gathering. The memory brought back some of the anger. She prayed before she spoke and asked whether the earlier boundary still fit. It did. She kept her answer brief and later talked with someone she trusted.

Exercise. Choose a passage to revisit when the memory returns. Write one short prayer and one practical action that still fits. If the circumstances change, give yourself time to reconsider what support or boundary would help.
Visual summary
Name what is yours to do
Arrange suitable support
Review the step you chose
Apply one step to a situation you face today.
Make your next step part of a larger practice

Choose one action for the week and one way to stay attentive to how it affects your conduct. Ask what would make the action easier to repeat. A regular prayer, a supportive conversation, or a written reminder can help you return to the same good purpose.

Martha kept her short boundary sentence and scheduled a check-in for the following week. She stopped rehearsing the longer answer she had first written. She continued to pray for Lydia and for wisdom about what to share. The family could take up the next ordinary gathering with clear expectations.
Use the One Faithful Step sheet. Write what you will do, who can support you, and when you will review it. Pray for Christ's compassion and patience as you take the next action you can carry.
Prayer. Lord Jesus, let Your compassion guide the step I take today. Give me patience to continue and wisdom to recognize when I need help. Amen.
Chapter 6 Prepare for a wise conversation
Give an appropriate conversation a clear purpose and a way to pause. Acknowledging a concern does not require an immediate embrace.
Read Scripture in its setting
Wherefore, my beloved brethren, let every man be swift to hear, slow to speak, slow to wrath: — James 1:19, KJV

James places a restraint on the speed of our speech and anger. Listening helps a conversation address the actual event, while a careful pause can prevent another injury. This instruction concerns your response. It cannot guarantee that a conversation will be safe or productive. Decide first whether contact belongs in the plan. If it does, give the discussion a clear purpose, an appropriate setting, and a way to stop or pause.
The practical situation

Martha considers a conversation that would explain the disclosure’s effect and ask for a particular correction. She does not need to make the discussion a complete trial of the relationship or promise immediate restored trust.
Biblical testimony · Nathan names a real wrong

Read 2 Samuel 12:1–13 in its historical setting. Nathan confronts David’s wrongdoing through an account that brings its moral seriousness into view. David acknowledges his sin. The narrative does not suggest that a truthful confrontation removes all consequences; the chapter continues with painful realities.

A modern reader should not assume Nathan’s particular commission or approach to a king authorizes an unsafe private confrontation. The useful lesson is clarity about the deed and the need for a truthful response. Prepare an account that can be checked, ask what needs to be understood, and involve appropriate people where authority or safety requires it.
Start with the action and its effect

Say what happened in terms you can verify. Describe how it affected you and make one request. Let the other person answer. If you need to correct a misunderstanding, return to the particular words or actions instead of arguing about the person's character.

Martha said that the financial detail had come up at dinner after she had asked for it to stay private. She explained that she felt exposed and asked Lydia to help stop the information from spreading. Lydia could respond to the exact request. Martha could ask a follow-up if something was unclear.

Exercise. Draft three sentences: one observation, one effect, and one request. Practice saying them quietly. If a sentence turns into a list of unrelated injuries, give those matters their own place in your notes or prayer.
Prepare to listen and to pause

Listening gives you a chance to understand what the person is saying before you respond. Repeat the point you heard and ask whether you understood it. If the conversation becomes too difficult to carry well, say when you need to stop or take time to think. You can return to a suitable conversation later if circumstances permit.

Martha heard Lydia begin to explain that she had meant to help. Martha waited for the explanation and asked whom Lydia had told. She was able to acknowledge the explanation and return to the request that it go no further. When the conversation drifted toward other family problems, she asked to keep it to the original issue.
Exercise. Write one listening question and one phrase you can use to pause. Choose a time to consider what happened before deciding what else to say or do.
Recognize when you have enough for the moment

A conversation may give you one answer and leave another issue open. End by stating the agreement you can confirm. If there is no agreement, state the boundary you can carry or say you need time. A clear ending reduces the chance of remembering different promises later.

Martha heard Lydia agree to speak with one relative. She thanked her and confirmed which detail she wanted kept private. She left the wider family discussion for another day. Later she made a short note of the specific agreement and gave herself time to see what happened.
Exercise. Before the conversation, decide what a clear ending might sound like. Afterward, record the action each person agreed to, if there was one. Choose a date to review what you can observe.
Visual summary
Decide whether contact is wise
State the action and effect
Listen, clarify, and pause as needed
Apply one step to a situation you face today.
Bring the conversation back to God

After speaking, pray about what you learned and the emotions that remain. Give thanks for a truthful exchange or the support you received. Ask for help with a boundary or a question still unresolved. If you need to speak with a trusted person, share the details appropriate to that conversation.

Martha felt both relieved and unsettled. She prayed about what Lydia had acknowledged and asked for patience as she waited to see whether the promise would be kept. She could return to her earlier plan for ordinary family contact and keep her private information private.
Use the Conversation Preparation sheet for an ordinary conflict where contact is appropriate. Pray for words that are truthful, gentle, and suited to the responsibility you can carry.
Chapter 7 Discern what repair would take
Repair should address the harm through observable action. Let reliable conduct, safety, and wisdom guide decisions about trust.
Read Scripture in its setting
For godly sorrow worketh repentance to salvation not to be repented of: but the sorrow of the world worketh death. — 2 Corinthians 7:10, KJV

Read 2 Corinthians 7:8–11 as Paul’s account of a particular letter and the Corinthians’ response. He distinguishes sorrow that leads into repentance from sorrow that does not produce that response. The passage invites attention to direction and conduct. It should not be used to diagnose a person’s mental health from their tears or to demand a public display of distress. Ask what wrong is acknowledged and what responsible action follows.
The practical situation
Martha considers whether the proposed repair addresses the disclosure. She can appreciate a useful step without treating one apology as proof that every form of trust should immediately return.
Biblical testimony · Zacchaeus names a concrete response

Read Luke 19:1–10. Jesus receives Zacchaeus, and the account includes a stated response concerning possessions and wrongful gain. The promised restitution is concrete and directed toward people affected by wrongdoing. It gives the reader a way to consider whether an apology reaches the actual harm.

The particular amount belongs to the account’s setting. A modern repair should fit the wrong, the responsibility, and the means genuinely available. Some harm cannot be fully reversed. An honest person can acknowledge that limit and still correct a false account, return property, or cooperate with an appropriate process. The person harmed remains free to consider what contact is wise.
Give changed conduct time to become visible

Paul describes the earnest response of the Corinthians after a painful letter. The passage places attention on what their sorrow produced. In an ordinary relationship, you can pay attention to what changes after an apology: whether a person keeps an agreement, honors a request, or takes responsibility when another concern arises.

Martha watched whether Lydia kept sensitive details private and followed through on the specific repair she had offered. Their ordinary contact continued at a level Martha could manage. Over time she had more information about what she was willing to share.
Exercise. Choose one observable behavior and a time to review it. Consider what an unchanged pattern would mean for your own choices. Keep the boundary that fits what you know today.
Separate different kinds of contact

You may be comfortable exchanging ordinary news and uncomfortable sharing sensitive information. You may be able to attend a gathering and prefer to leave a private discussion for another time. Think about the kinds of access or conversation that are appropriate to the evidence and your circumstances.

Martha could greet Lydia at dinner and help with preparations. She still kept financial matters private. She did not have to make one decision that applied to every aspect of their relationship. That allowed her to keep the form of contact she had chosen without going further than she could carry.

Exercise. Name the contact you are comfortable with, the information you will keep private, and the support you want. Consider whether these choices need to be communicated. Set a date to review them for yourself.
Respond when the promised repair does not happen

An offer of repair may remain unfinished. If it is appropriate and safe, ask one clear question about what was agreed and whether it has happened. Then decide what you can do based on the answer and the conduct you observe. Give yourself room to continue an existing boundary.

Martha asked whether Lydia had spoken to the relative. Lydia had made the call but had not reached them. They agreed that Lydia could try once more and let Martha know. If nothing changed, Martha would keep her existing boundary and decide separately whether a direct request to the relative made sense.
Exercise. Write a follow-up sentence about one concrete agreement. Decide what action is yours if you receive no reply or the repair remains incomplete. Take any further contact decisions with care.
Visual summary
Identify the harm acknowledged

A useful review names what happened, what remains unclear, and what next step belongs to each person. You can appreciate a sincere action while giving the relationship time to develop. A small verified change gives you something specific to thank God for.

Lydia eventually reached the relative and asked them to leave the matter private. Martha thanked her for keeping the commitment. Chapter 8 Return to forgiveness when hurt resurfaces
A reminder can be brought into prayer again. Trusted company and a useful return plan can support continuing practice.
Read Scripture in its setting
Trust in him at all times; ye people, pour out your heart before him: God is a refuge for us. Selah. — Psalm 62:8, KJV

The psalm gives trust and honest prayer a place together. Read verses 5–8 and notice the repeated attention to God as refuge. Returning to prayer when hurt resurfaces does not require pretending that no reminder occurred. Ask whether you are facing an old memory, new information, or a fresh harmful action. Those matters may call for different practical responses while each can be brought truthfully before God.
The practical situation

Martha has a plan for a difficult reminder. She can pause, pray, return to an appropriate boundary, and ask a trusted person for support. A new injury is assessed as a new event rather than dismissed merely because she has chosen forgiveness before.
Biblical testimony · Peter is given work after failure

Read John 21:15–19 alongside the accounts of Peter’s denial. The risen Jesus addresses Peter and entrusts him with responsibility. The encounter belongs to Peter’s particular calling, and its words should be heard in that setting. It also shows that failure does not need to become the only sentence through which a person understands every future day.

If you need to own a wrong in your response, confess it and make an appropriate correction. If you are carrying another person’s harm, do not take responsibility for conduct that was not yours. Ask which faithful task lies before you now. Returning to a useful responsibility can coexist with an ongoing need for support and protection.
Review whether the boundary still serves its purpose

A boundary can continue to fit after circumstances change. It may also need a practical adjustment. Ask what it protects, whether you have been able to keep it, and what help would make it easier to carry. Give yourself time before changing a form of contact or access.

Martha realized that keeping her finances private was still useful. Muting the family chat all week had made it difficult to see ordinary announcements. She adjusted when she checked the chat and kept the subject boundary. The new arrangement protected what mattered and let her remain connected.
Exercise. Write what your current boundary protects. Name one place where keeping it has been hard. Choose whether to keep it, adjust one practical feature, or ask for support before deciding.
Let trustworthy people see what helps

Support can become more useful when you can describe the part that made a difference. Thank the person for what they did and tell them what would help next time. A supporter can listen, remind you of a plan you chose, or help you reach an appropriate person.

Martha told her relative that the private check-in after dinner had helped. She asked whether they could have another short conversation after the next family gathering. Her relative said they could talk the following morning. They agreed on a time that both could keep.
Exercise. Name one part of the support you received and how it helped. If you need further help, make a specific request. Give the other person room to say what they can offer.
Notice the good you can carry now

Returning to forgiveness may involve ordinary conduct: declining to share a humiliating story, speaking truthfully about a boundary, praying for someone, or asking for accountability through a suitable channel. Give each action its own place. You can see progress in how you respond while still praying about the hurt.

Martha noticed that she could take part in a family meal without rehearsing a reply all afternoon. She still kept the boundary she had chosen. She thanked God for one evening in which she had been able to enjoy a conversation and leave the private matter alone.
Exercise. Write one choice you made that reflected patience, truth, or mercy. Say what helped you carry it. Use that detail to prepare for a similar moment next week.

Martha kept a short prayer, her private boundary, and the option to ask someone to listen. She thanked God for Lydia's practical step and for the patience to give trust time. At the next review she could return to what she actually knew and decide what she was willing to carry.
